mclm.def: Purpose backed by governance rather than declared is credible, so stakeholders make firm-specific investments they would otherwise withhold. Below the threshold of credibility, purpose is cheap talk.
mclm.name: commitment_credibility

mclm.def: Enfranchising more stakeholders raises the informational and deliberative burden on the central authority, and does so at an increasing rate.
mclm.name: decision_cost

mclm.def: Joint decision-making generates honest mistakes from lack of expertise, information or talent among the principals.
mclm.name: principal_competence_cost

mclm.def: Principals decide in their own interest against the interests of others, which is the opportunism stakeholders anticipate and price in.
mclm.name: principal_conflict_cost

mclm.def: The classical agency problem: managers pursue their own agenda, and a wider enfranchisement gives them more room to play principals off against each other.
mclm.name: agent_conflict_cost

mclm.def: Determines what fraction of what stakeholders are owed can be specified ex ante, and therefore held as control rather than residual rights.
mclm.name: contractibility

mclm.def: AI intensity raises contractibility: more of what is conceded can be written down and verified ex ante, so the control channel widens.
mclm.name: ai_contractibility_shift

mclm.def: AI lowers the cost of monitoring agents, reducing agent-side conflict costs.
mclm.name: ai_agency_cost_reduction

mclm.def: Principal costs are charged against the residual channel only, never the control channel. Residual rights are the ones exercised at discretion, so the cost of a principal deciding badly falls there.
mclm.name: principal_cost_incidence

mclm.def: Agency costs are charged against both channels, because delegation degrades what is contracted as well as what is left to discretion.

base.name: Control costs and partitioned rights
base.what: The governance literature the two-channel model reads for the quantities the purpose literature does not state: who exercises control, what that costs on each side of the relation, and whether rights to one resource can be held in partitions by several stakeholders at once. Two papers, read in by hand on 25 October 2026. A literature of two papers is a thin literature and the bench scores it as one: nothing here is corroborated more than twice, and the one place where both papers say the same thing is the only corroborated relation in it.

papers.title: Principal costs: A new theory for corporate law and governance
Towards a property rights foundation for a stakeholder theory of the firm

constructs.definition: The share of a firm's control rights that investors hand to managers while voluntarily restricting their own, which is the position the firm occupies on what the paper calls the governance spectrum.
Losses from honest mistakes made by investors who exercise control, attributable to a lack of expertise, information or talent rather than to any divergence of interest.
Losses from investor self-seeking, which arise where principals share control, cash flows or both, and which conventional agency theory leaves out.
Losses from honest mistakes made by managers who exercise delegated control, for the same three reasons and with no divergence of interest implied.
Losses from manager self-seeking under the separation of ownership and control, which is the single quantity conventional agency theory treats as the governance problem.
The sum of the four control costs, principal and agent, competence and conflict. The quantity the paper says an optimal governance structure minimizes, as against minimizing the agent side alone.

Whether one governance structure is best for every firm, or whether the best structure depends on the firm. The only construct in this literature that two papers reach, which is why it is the only relation here with any corroboration behind it.
The extent to which rights to one resource are held in partitions by several different people rather than whole by one, so that a stakeholder can hold a facet of a resource without owning it.

Whether ownership is located in residual rights to income, as classical property rights theory has it, or in residual control rights, as the modern literature has it. The paper ties the first to ex ante contractual problems and the second to ex post ones.

The fraction of what a stakeholder is owed that can be stipulated by contract in advance and therefore held as a fixed control right, as against left to whoever holds the residual. RECONSTRUCTED, and carried by no paper here: Stoelhorst and Vishwanathan (2024) distinguish fixed from residual control rights and make contractually stipulated fixed rights for vulnerable stakeholders the distinctive instrument of the stakeholder corporation, but they state the distinction as a kind and not as a quantity. Read here as a degree, because a model that moves between the two channels needs a margin and not a category. The inference is this scenario's and not the paper's.

claims.quote: Investors who delegate control to managers, and restrict their own control rights, avoid principal costs
claims.scope: business firms choosing a division of control between investors and managers; the paper's referent throughout is American corporate law

claims.quote: Delegation raises the competence of whoever decides, which is what lowers principal competence costs
claims.scope: business firms choosing a division of control between investors and managers

claims.quote: Agent costs are produced when managers exercise control
claims.scope: business firms choosing a division of control between investors and managers

claims.quote: Managers make honest mistakes of their own, which generate agent competence costs
claims.scope: business firms choosing a division of control between investors and managers

claims.quote: Total control costs are the sum of the four categories, principal and agent, competence and conflict
claims.scope: any business firm; the decomposition is offered as general

claims.quote: Because the division of control that minimises total control costs varies by firm, no governance structure is intrinsically best
claims.scope: business firms; argued against uniform reform prescriptions in American corporate law

claims.quote: Rights to one resource can be held in partitions by many different people, so ownership is a bundle of rights rather than a physical thing
claims.scope: the firm as a method of property tenure, examined stakeholder by stakeholder

claims.quote: There may not be a single best governance structure
claims.scope: unstated; offered as a programmatic conclusion rather than for a stated population

theses.says: Corporate law should let each firm choose its own division of control, because the cost-minimising division is firm-specific and uniform prescriptions therefore misfire.
Incomplete and implicit contracting in modern property rights theory is the economic foundation a stakeholder theory of the firm needs, and the work of building it had not been done.

declarations.name: fixed control rights, share of what is owed
declarations.note: Reconstructed from Stoelhorst and Vishwanathan (2024), who distinguish fixed control rights from residual ones and take fixed rights for vulnerable stakeholders seriously as an instrument, without stating the split as a quantity. Declared here as a degree on [0, 1] so that a model can move between the two channels continuously. No paper in either literature asserts this quantity, and it is recorded as a declaration rather than carried as a claim for that reason.
